description:
Like our team name, the earth is also subject-to-change

NISAR helps us view those changes on our planet
summary:
We built a web application to make NISAR’s data as accessible as possible to researchers, hobbyists, and enthusiasts. Our project dramatically reduces friction in the existing data access pipelines, and also makes it easy to bring in other open-source earth science data into the same analysis. We hope that it will enable a wide range of people to visualize, appreciate, and build on the existing wealth of data from NISAR. 

The application itself presents a fully interactable map interface. Users can select areas, draw contours, and click points to simply and painlessly find the data they want. The interface allows them to select between the different data processing levels available, quickly scrub through time stamps, make comparisons against other datasets, and easily save their findings. 

Using our application and the NISAR data, we found a number of interesting stories unfolding on the Earth’s surface including active volcanoes, flowing glaciers, sinking landscapes, landslides, and agricultural activity. We’ve compiled these areas for your viewing pleasure. We look forward to seeing many more years of NISAR data, and we hope that our application will enable the next generation of scientists and storytellers to make the best use of it.
details:
Our application is basically “Google Maps for NISAR”. The data from NISAR is valuable, but its pre-packaging as large HDF5 files makes it somewhat difficult to deal with. The Alaskan Satellite Facility's interactive map is useful, but it leaves some features to be desired. We initially set out to build this application just as an internal tool to make our lives easier while working with the NISAR data for this project, but quickly realized that our interface could make other people’s lives easier too.

From a technical perspective, the application’s backend is a Flask app written in Python with a SQLite database. The frontend is a React app written in JSX. The default map visualization is pulled from ArcGIS Online with the Esri World Imagery set. OpenStreetMap and NASA GIBS world maps are also included, selectable from a drop down. From the webapp, the user can navigate freely around the map. They can request data by clicking a point on the map, by selecting an area, or by drawing a contour. The relevant NISAR granules are identified through NASA’s CMR service and then downloaded from the ASF. Using HTTP range requests, the relevant pixels for each study site are pulled from the HDF5 files and processed into map images and per-pass measurements (such as open-water fraction and backscatter). The whole site supports WCAG keyboard navigation, and ships with a guided tour to walk users through their first visit.

There are a number of tangible benefits to our application. First and foremost, we believe that its interface and tools are much more accessible to the average user. The point-and-click modality makes it easy to grab the right data, and the menus greatly simplify the processing level and time selections. One feature that we’re particularly pleased with is the mosaic tiling mode. If the user selects an area which is not fully covered by a single pass, they can choose to load as many passes as necessary to fully tile their target area. They can also scrub through time to see each pass in context. In addition to ease-of-use, the explanatory tooltips and sidebars provide useful insights and information on what the NISAR data actually represents. To the layperson, terms like “GCOV” and  “Interferogram” are not very descriptive. We aim to provide enough context to help anyone, regardless of their technical familiarity, understand the data and make use of it. And finally, the stories we’ve compiled provide a useful jumping-off-point for new users. They highlight some of the most interesting ways that the NISAR data can be used, and will hopefully inspire users to go hunting for more.
